hops.afterHeading: Which protein? A screen, and the claim it refused to make
hops.title: A year of dead ends before Piezo1
hops.text: Bertrand Coste spent a year poking mouse Neuro2A cells with a glass probe while silencing candidate membrane-protein genes one at a time. Starting from roughly three hundred possible candidates, he worked through dozens with no luck: knock one down, poke the cell, and the current still fired. More than seventy candidates into the screen, silencing a little-studied gene called Fam38A finally made the poke-evoked current drop sharply. Ardem Patapoutian, who ran the lab, later recalled that Coste walked into his office very calmly and said, "I found it." They named the protein Piezo1, after the Greek word for pressure.

sources.citation: Ardem Patapoutian – Biographical, The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021, NobelPrize.org
Scientific Background: Discoveries of Receptors for Temperature and Touch (Advanced Information), The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021, NobelPrize.org

hops.afterHeading: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve
hops.title: How bacteria survive a rain shower
hops.text: When the salt outside a bacterium suddenly drops, as in a rain shower on salty soil, water floods in and the swelling cell stretches its membrane toward bursting. Escherichia coli relies mainly on two of seven stretch-gated channels. MscS activates at lower tension than MscL, which opens just short of cell rupture; in lab tests, cells lacking both fared much worse. In E. coli membrane patches, MscL reaches half activation near 10.4 mN/m, with an estimated in-plane area gain of about 20 nm² inferred from activation curves. At that tension, T × ΔA comes to roughly 50 k_BT, just enough to make open and closed equally likely.

hops.afterHeading: Reading a patch: from pressure to current, and back to an area
hops.title: The small bubble empties into the big one
hops.text: Join a small soap bubble to a big one through a tube, open the valve, and you might expect them to even out. They do not. The small bubble shrinks and blows its air into the big one until it is gone. For a soap film at fixed surface tension, the pressure inside rises as the radius shrinks, so the tight little sphere pushes harder. A patch under a pipette obeys the same geometry, read the other way round: the suction alone does not set the tension, because the dome's curvature changes it too. That is why Lewis and Grandl imaged every patch instead of trusting the pressure dial.

sources.citation: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Section 11.8: Cohesion and Adhesion in Liquids: Surface Tension and Capillary Action

image.caption: Pressure in a curved film depends on its radius, so pressure alone cannot tell you a patch's tension.

audio.title: Tarantula venom, a jumping variant and a bladder sensor
audio.transcript:
Mechanotransduction can sound like pure lab physics, all domes and bilayers and patch pipettes. Yet the same channels turn up in odd corners of biology, from tarantula venom to vertical jumps to knowing when to find a bathroom.

Start with the Chilean rose tarantula. Its venom contains a short peptide called G s M T x four that inhibits about eighty percent of Piezo one's mechanically evoked current in patches. A drug that depends on a precise fit behaves like a right hand in a right-handed glove, so its mirror image usually fits poorly and loses activity. When researchers built the mirror-image version of G s M T x four, though, it inhibited Piezo one like the natural spider peptide. That broke the lock-and-key rule. The leading model is that the peptide does not plug the pore at all. It rests shallowly in the outer layer of the membrane, and when the membrane stretches it slips deeper, taking up more room among the lipids and easing some of the tension the channel feels.

Next, consider what happens when a Piezo channel takes a little longer to shut off. In two thousand eighteen, researchers found a gain-of-function variant of Piezo one, called E seven fifty-six del, in about a third of people in African populations. In cultured cells it inactivated more slowly than usual, and in the dish, donor red blood cells carrying it were dehydrated and showed reduced infection by the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. That looked like a neat story, and then it got messier. In two thousand twenty, a case-control study of children in Gabon found that one copy of the variant was strongly associated with protection against severe malaria, yet in a separate lab test, red cells from donors with one copy held a normal amount of water and supported normal parasite growth. Once infected, those cells displayed less of a parasite protein called P f E M P one, which gave the researchers another explanation to test. Then a larger study in Ghana did not replicate the Gabon association. The same variant also turned up somewhere unexpected. Tendon cells use Piezo one to sense collagen fibers sliding past each other, and in rodents more Piezo one activity made tendons stiffer. In people, researchers compared each volunteer's one-legged jump after a short drop with that same person's one-legged jump from the floor. In carriers, the drop jump averaged about a hundred and eleven percent of the floor jump; in non-carriers, about ninety-eight percent. One small change in a channel's timing, and two stories about it that are still being worked out.

Finally, it is easy to think of Piezo two as a touch sensor for fingertips. In two thousand twenty, a team including Ardem Patapoutian and Alexander Chesler found that Piezo two helps mice sense bladder filling, and traced its role to cells in the bladder lining and to the sensory nerves that serve the bladder. They also studied twelve people with inactivating Piezo two variants, ages five to forty-three, who answered questions about urination. Healthy people typically go five or six times a day. All twelve went less often, as rarely as once or twice a day regardless of how much they drank. Most said they could spend an entire day without feeling the need to go, so they followed a schedule instead of an urge, and many also described sudden urgency. It is a real difference in daily life, and it shows how much quiet work this channel does.

From a spider's lipid cushion to a signal from your own bladder, mechanical force is running far more of your physiology than touch alone.
